title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription service allegedly recorded work conversations without participant knowledge and used them to train its AI systems by default. The company's privacy policy included a checkbox for consent, but users claim they were unaware their conversations would be recorded and shared. This is a deployment problem: a system that processes sensitive data was configured to use it for training purposes without ensuring all affected parties understood or agreed to this use.

The lawsuit alleges that Otter de-identifies data before training on it, but questions whether this process actually removes confidential information. It is not established whether the de-identification was inadequate, whether users genuinely could not find the consent mechanism, or whether Otter's technical practices violated applicable law. A court allowed the privacy claims to proceed, meaning the allegations are not dismissed as legally unfounded, but no ruling or verdict has been reached.

This shows the gap between a technical disclosure mechanism and actual informed consent at scale. Catching this would have required either obtaining explicit consent from all meeting participants before recording, or designing the system to record only when everyone present had actively agreed, rather than relying on the meeting organizer's checkbox in a policy document.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence company, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The company's Otter Notebook service, which transcribes virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Microsoft Teams, allegedly records and shares conversations with Otter to train its AI systems by default, without notifying meeting participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter was covertly recording confidential conversations. The lawsuit argues that while Otter's privacy policy mentions user consent through a checkbox, many people remain unaware their conversations are being used this way.

The case raises significant privacy concerns as approximately 25 million people use Otter's transcription tools, which have processed over 1 billion meetings since the company's founding in 2016. Previous incidents include an AI researcher whose confidential business details were transcribed and shared, and concerns from journalists interviewing human rights activists about potential access by foreign governments. Otter claims it de-identifies data before using it for AI training, but the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information. The suit seeks class-action status to represent California residents whose private conversations were unknowingly shared with Otter for financial gain.
